title: Strengthened second law for periodic processes
authors: Jake Schaefer, Ben Ansbacher, Jan Korbel, David H. Wolpert
abstract: Many physical systems evolve under periodic driving: the same control protocol is applied again and again, even though the state of the system itself need not return to where it started after each cycle. We derive a physics-independent lower bound on the entropy production of \emph{any} periodic process modeled by the evolution of an initial distribution $p_0$ by a repeated application of the same map $G$. This is a strict strengthening of the second law of thermodynamics for periodic processes. It does not require that the single-period dynamics arise from a CTMC, satisfy (local) detailed balance, or be subject to other typical restrictions. We discuss its application to spins in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata, with possible extensions to other uniform computers.
summary: This paper derives a strict, physics-independent lower bound on the entropy production for any system undergoing periodic driving. By analyzing the Mismatch Cost (MMC) over multiple cycles, the authors establish a generalized second law applicable to diverse systems like spin models and digital automata. This result significantly strengthens current understanding of non-equilibrium thermodynamics in time-periodic settings.
main_problem: Deriving a physics-independent lower bound on the entropy production for any periodic process, strengthening the standard second law of thermodynamics.
main_result: A lower bound on entropy production is established using the Mismatch Cost (MMC) that depends only on the initial distribution and the driving map, regardless of the underlying physical details.
method: The analysis uses the Mismatch Cost (MMC) decomposition of a general thermodynamic cost function, optimizing over all possible prior distributions to find a minimal dissipation bound.
model_or_system: The framework applies to general stochastic processes evolving under periodic driving, modeled by repeatedly applying a stochastic map G. Specific applications include the Curie-Weiss model (Ising spins) and Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA).
key_observables: Entropy Production ($\Sigma_t$), Mismatch Cost (MMC), and the periodic-optimal prior ($ ar{q}$).
important_parameters: The periodicity of the driving process, the initial distribution $p_0$, and the map $G$.
main_assumptions: The process is modeled by the repeated application of a single map G, and the analysis relies on the general structure of the MMC decomposition.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the general MMC decomposition, then specializing this to periodic processes, and finally applying the derived bounds to specific physical models like the Curie-Weiss model and DFAs.
why_interesting: The derivation of a universal, physics-independent bound on entropy production for periodic systems provides a powerful new tool for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, extending beyond standard Markovian assumptions.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Visualization of spin system. Spins coupled to each bath at inverse temperatures β1, β2, and exchange heats Q1, Q2 over time. Each reservoir pushes probability distribu- tion over configurations p(σ) to its own Boltzmann distribu- tion. Thus, in the stationary state for the combined dynamics summed over the reservoirs, there will still be nonzero current, giving a nonequilibrium steady state.

FIG. 2. Minimal dissipation, MMC at the EP-optimal prior (4), total EP, and nonadiabatic EP as a function of time elapsed for the spin system starting at p0. The long-term minimal dissipation D(p0||π) is plotted as a horizontal dotted line. The total variation distance between the current distri- bution and the NESS dTV(pt, π) is plotted in a separate plot in solid cyan. We see the minimal dissipation is a significant portion of the total EP, whereupon after reaching the fixed point (NESS), the minimal dissipation saturates and residual cost dominates — growing the total EP without bound.

FIG. 3. Heatmap displaying, for different times T, the ratio of minimal dissipation to total entropy production MT /ΣT as a function of the coupling strength J ∈[−0.5, 0.5] and inverse temperature of the second bath β2 ∈[0, 8.0], where the first bath is fixed at β1 = 3.0 as in the main text. For a large fraction of parameter space, and in particular the anti-ferromagnetic regime, the minimal dissipation is a significant fraction of the total EP.

FIG. 4. (Left) Minimal dissipation MN(¯q) for four different DFAs that all recognize the same language, at different input distributions (p, 1 −p). (Far right) Minimal DFA for recognizing binary representations of integers divisible by three. The initial state is 0 and the accept state is also 0. In the long time limit, the minimal dissipation scales monotonically with the number of redundant states, while in the short time limit there can be crossovers.

FIG. 5. Heatmap of MN(q; p0) over the simplex for various values of N for the D3 DFA. Here, p = 0.1. The color coding shows the periodic MMC for choosing any other prior q ̸= ¯q. The white lines represent the trajectory of the POP up until the N-th iteration, indicated by the white dot. The color scale indicates the periodic MMC using any prior other than the POP. Note at N = 1, the POP is just p0.
